articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled

A spokesman for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed Monday that the group had carried out new attacks over the preceding 48 hours on Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesman, said in a statement shared on social media that the group had struck Saudi Arabia's eastern Dammam Airport  "using two drones, and the operation achieved its objective successfully, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport."
He said another drone hit an "early warning radar in Jizan," a city on Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast, while unspecified Houthi weapons hit "a military transport aircraft at Jizan Airport."
The Houthis have peppered Saudi Arabia's airports and energy infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of Yemen's government in the impoverished Middle Eastern nation's grueling decade-long civil war. Iran has long backed the Houthis as a powerful proxy force, particularly as a counter to Iran's arch-foe Saudi Arabia, which shares a long border with Yemen.
Houthi drone and missile strikes last month killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports , and despite the kingdom's vast military and financial advantage over the rebels, it has been unable to stop the attacks .
There was no immediate information from Saudi officials to confirm or deny Saree's claims on Monday.
The Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday, Iranian state media reported, in a continuation of recent talks between the two countries about the situation in the Middle East.
During their call, Rezaei and Putin discussed regional and global affairs, focusing on West Asia and ongoing "strategic cooperation" between Iran and Russia, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Iran and Russia have long been allies, and their relationship has been cemented during both the ongoing Russian assault on Ukraine, and the U.S. war with Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in October that Tehran's ties with Russia were closer than ever, contradicting Mr. Trump's assertion at the time that Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Tehran amid the war.
According to Tasnim, Rezaei thanked Putin Monday for Russia's support.
Iran's top diplomat said Monday that negotiations with the U.S., via mediators, aimed at reaching an agreement to end the war have been "proceeding very intensively," but he added that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality," according to Iran's state news agency IRNA.
IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as reiterating that Tehran will not back down from its conditions for a deal to end the war and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Closed-door negotiations have taken place via mediators, primarily Qatar and Pakistan, and Iranian officials said earlier Monday that it would be up to the U.S. side to make a move and end the monthslong standoff sparked by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
"If they choose honest diplomacy, we are ready to engage," IRNA quoted Araghchi as saying. "If they intend to deceive us and launch military operations, they will face a response more bitter and forceful than before."
The Iranian Navy claimed Monday that another oil tanker had caught on fire after striking a sea mine near the eastern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency, which is closely linked with Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The report cited the Navy as saying the unnamed vessel had struck a mine while attempting to use shipping lanes through the strait that Iran considers unauthorized and unsafe, but which the Trump administration and U.S. military have repeatedly claimed are free and open.
The tanker had switched off its navigation systems, Fars said, referring to a common practice by commercial vessels trying to obscure their movements in the region.
Tanker owners should take a lesson from the fate of vessels that violate Iran's rules by trying to transit the strait without authorization from Tehran, the report cited the navy as saying.
On Friday, despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that the southern shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe to navigate, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region in the month of October alone, a record high.
The Iranian regime said earlier Monday that 11 ships had "caught fire" in or near the Strait of Hormuz in the last nine days alone.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran had presented Qatari mediators with a proposal to shorten the implementation period of a potential deal with the U.S. to just two days from seven.
In an interview with Al Jazeera , Araghchi said: "The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days."
The Iranian minister added, however, that Tehran's conditions for a deal to end the war remain the same.
The Islamic Republic regime has demanded that the U.S. release frozen Iranian financial assets, lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports, as well as sanctions, and cease hostilities on all fronts, including Israel's battle with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. In exchange, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping traffic and commit to further talks on its nuclear program.
Under the original seven-day implementation proposed by Tehran, the Strait of Hormuz would have been reopened on the sixth day.
With the shortened implementation period, according to a statement on the Iranian government website, "a series of measures will be taken by the United States on the first day, and on the second day, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and maritime traffic will return to its previous conditions."
Iran's government-run broadcaster IRIB said Monday that 11 oil tankers had "caught fire" in the Strait of Hormuz in the previous nine days, disputing U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper's assertion last week that "all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."
In a post on X, IRIB said the 11 tankers had caught on fire since Oct. 25, the day on which it claimed Cooper made his recent fly-over of the strait.
The Iranian network offered no evidence, but claimed some of the vessels sank "to the depths of the sea."
Since the start of the war in February, Iran has targeted vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to assert control over the narrow waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's crude oil supply typically passed prior to the conflict.
Cooper said last week in a Friday video statement that he saw no Iranian navy vessels in the strait during his flyover earlier in the week.
Later Friday, however, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the month of October alone, a record high.
The U.S. military and President Trump have repeatedly declared Iran's navy destroyed and insisted that southern shipping lanes through the strait are available to merchant vessels, but ongoing Iranian threats and attacks have kept the risks and costs for shippers high, which has helped Tehran keep maintain pressure on global energy prices.
Iranian officials repeated warnings Monday of possible gas shortages for residents ahead of the winter, and they called on people to conserve the resource.

articles.title_orig: Stocks jump as oil prices tumble before midterms, tech shares rebound: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks jump as oil prices tumble before midterms, tech shares rebound: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as senior U.S. and Iranian officials signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 7.3% to $105.14 a barrel as of 11:25 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate declined about 7% to $96.87 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections.
The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Meanwhile, Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to the state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency .
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings
articles.title_zh: China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings
articles.content_orig:
China is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East, including over the US-Israel war on Iran , following a lapse in activity.
Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Monday met a senior Iranian security official in Beijing, while President Xi Jinping hosted Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq for a landmark state visit.
Wang told Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, that dialogue and negotiation remained “the only viable path forward” as conflicts in the region “drag on and risk further spillover”.
He also reaffirmed China’s support for Iran’s sovereignty and security. Beijing has consistently blamed the US and Israel for starting the conflict.
“China is very close to Tehran; it is the biggest trading partner of Iran, the biggest customer of Iranian crude,” said Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing.
However, Beijing’s diplomacy efforts have recently been stalled, she noted.
“It’s been a few weeks or even months [in which] China really hasn’t done much diplomatically towards … ending the war,” Yu said.
The meetings on Monday appear to illustrate that China is growing impatient with the lack of progress.
“I think China is very frustrated, and it wants to be seen to enter [the process],” Yu said.
Reflecting the step up in activity, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday that Zhai Jun, Beijing’s special envoy on the Middle East, will visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month.
Meanwhile, Xi received Sultan Haitham, the first Omani head of state to visit China since the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1978.
The Chinese president said the Middle East and Gulf “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict”.
Sitting across from Iran on the Strait of Hormuz, Oman is a key player in navigation on the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of global energy exports traversed before the US-Iran war restricted traffic.
China is one of the world’s largest energy importers. Xi described bilateral ties with Oman as being at a “new historical starting point”.
During the visit, China and Oman signed 14 cooperation documents, covering areas including artificial intelligence, green energy and supply chains, along with a currency swap agreement.
In a joint statement, they called for safe navigation to resume through Hormuz and urged the US and Iran to restart dialogue.
Yu said the conflict had made the relationship “more of a priority for both sides”, particularly given the disruption to China’s energy imports.
“Oman is particularly important because many of its ports are outside the strait,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Oil Prices Slide on Mideast Hopes; Stocks Rebound After Friday's Selloff
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Oil Prices Slide on Mideast Hopes; Stocks Rebound After Friday's Selloff
articles.content_orig:
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: The Bull And Male Donkey Who Choose Each Other Again And Again (For Sex)
articles.title_zh: The Bull And Male Donkey Who Choose Each Other Again And Again (For Sex)
articles.content_orig:
By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR
Published: 11:00 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 11:00 EDT, 2 November 2026
Scientists have discovered an 'unusual sexual bond' between a bull and a male donkey, with the animals repeatedly choosing each other – despite having plenty of females around them.
The unusual partnership involves a bull called Achille and a male donkey called Patroclo, who both live on an Ethiopian plateau.
Scientists from the University of Pisa first spotted a sexual interaction between the two animals while they were in the field conducting another study.
Subsequent observations showed that the two males repeatedly chose each other, even though they belonged to different owners and only saw one another during time in the pasture.
'The sexual interactions between Achille, the bull, and Patroclo, the male donkey, were not isolated events,' said Elisabetta Palagi, an author of the study.
'What really caught our attention was that these interactions were embedded in a very selective and consistent social relationship between the two individuals.'
Scientists have discovered an 'unusual sexual bond' between a bull and a male donkey, with the animals repeatedly choosing each other – despite having plenty of females to choose from
During the first interaction, the team observed Achille mounting Patroclo.
Normally, this kind of behaviour would result in an animal trying to kick or act defensively.
However, this wasn't the case, with Patroclo happily accepting Achille's advances.
'They repeatedly chose to stay close to each other and engaged in many different affiliative behaviors, such as licking, rubbing, and nuzzling, alongside the repeated mounting behavior,' explained study author André da Cruz.
'Importantly, this was happening in a social environment where both animals had access to other potential partners, including individuals of both sexes and of their own species.'
This wasn't a one–off encounter. In total, the team saw 51 mountings between the animals from March 6 to March 19.
During other romps, Patroclo would present his hindquarters to Achille, and nipped him.
On two occassions, Achille did mount another male donkey.
However, that animal showed 'clear avoidance behaviours', including flattened ears and threatening expressions.
During the first interaction, the team observed Achille mounting Patroclo. Normally, this kind of behaviour would result in an animal trying to kick or act defensively. However, this wasn't the case, with Patroclo happily accepting Achille's advances
Martina Francesconi, lead author of the study, said: 'We believe the key finding is not simply that a bull mounted a male donkey.
'It is that this unusual sexual behavior was part of a broader, selective social relationship.
'Our observations suggest that it cannot be easily explained simply by a lack of alternative mating opportunities, although we cannot say from this study exactly what function these sexual interactions may have had.'
The researchers now hope to carry out further studies to understand the relationship dynamic further.
'For us, a major question for future research is what mechanisms, and possibly what benefits, might underlie these interactions,' Ms Palagi says.
'Are they mainly related to social bonding? Could they play a role in maintaining relationships or reducing tension? Or do they emerge from a combination of social and sexual motivations?
'We think that comparative research across species with different social systems could help us distinguish between these possibilities.'
'More broadly, we would like to better understand how social relationships shape sexual behavior and how behavioral flexibility allows animals to navigate complex social environments.
'We see this study as a starting point for asking these broader questions.'
Homosexuality in nature has been observed in as many as 1,500 animal species, humans included.
There has yet to be an accepted explanation based on neurological, chemical or behavioural factors to explain why some animals are homosexual and some are heterosexual.
Some scientists say it may be due to exposure to testosterone levels in the womb, although this remains a hotly debated topic which has yet to be proved.
In a book titled: 'Homosexual Behaviour in Animals: An Evolutionary Perspective', the author, UCL professor Dr Volker Sommer, writes: 'Within a select number of species, homosexual activity is widespread and occurs at levels that approach or sometimes even surpass heterosexual activity.'
Homosexual behaviour has been observed in many animals, including macaques, dwarf chimpanzees, lions, giraffes, dolphins, orcas and humans.
Some studies claim homosexuality may be as common as being found in up to 95 percent of all animal species.
There are two principal schools of thought when it comes to the prevalence of homosexuality in nature.
One theory states that homosexuality in animals doesn't need an explanation, with animals being homosexual just as naturally as they are heterosexual.
It appears irrational for it to survive as a trait as it hinders the ability to procreate directly, but many speculate it allows individuals to ensure their genetic material is passed down the generations indirectly as they are able to look after members of their family with offspring.
For example, helping nurture the offspring of a sister.
Similar behaviour dedicated to the 'greater good' of a large group have been seen in various species.
For example, in familial wolf packs only one pair of animals breeds – the alpha and the beta. The other animals ensure the protection, feeding and nurturing of the litter.
This allows their genetic material to pass indirectly to the next generation through their sister, brother, mother etc or whatever the relationship may be.
The same school of thought applies to animals which have exceeded their reproductive age.
For example, female elephants which are now too old to have offspring.
They still play a crucial role in the protection of the young – the matriarch leads the group to spots of food, water and chases off would-be predators.
These actions ensure the survival of the young and vulnerable members of her family, again helping ensure her genetic material is passed down through the generations indirectly.
A similar concept can be applied to homosexuality, some experts claim.
Without the ability to reproduce directly, they are able to expend energy looking after the offspring of their family members.
Another theory states that homosexual behaviours aid in the successful passing on of genes in the long term as young animals 'practise' mating techniques and ways of attracting a member of the opposite sex.
Rates of homosexuality in different species continues to be unknown, as ongoing research finds more nuances to homosexuality in nature.
It continues to be found in more species but the level of homosexuality in individual species is not well enough studied to be able to determine if homosexuality is becoming increasingly common.

articles.title_orig: China Presses Forward on Human Moon Landing Before 2030
articles.title_zh: China Presses Forward on Human Moon Landing Before 2030
articles.content_orig:
Image credit: CCTV/Inside Outer Space screengrab
China continues to chart its first crewed Moon landing before 2030, detailing current plans last weekend during the Seventh Manned Space Symposium in Beijing.
The two-day symposium drew more than 800 experts and scholars to explore how digital and intelligent technologies can advance human spaceflight.
Uncrewed test flights of the Mengzhou crewed spacecraft and the Lanyue lunar lander are planned ahead of a crewed Moon landing mission.
Wang Xiang, deputy chief designer of China’s manned space program, said a trio of astronauts will carry out the Moon mission, with two individuals landing on the lunar surface.
Image credit: CCTV/Inside Outer Space screengrab
“We will use the unmanned Lanyue lunar lander to verify all the key technologies throughout the entire crewed process as much as possible – including launch, entering the lunar orbit, rendezvous and docking with the Mengzhou spacecraft, landing and staying on the lunar surface, taking off again and re-docking with the crewed spaceship Mengzhou, so as to make sure the crewed flight will be safe and reliable,” Wang told China Central Television (CCTV).
Two Long March-10 carrier rockets will launch the Lanyue lunar lander and the Mengzhou spaceship in succession, then the two will conduct a rendezvous and docking in lunar orbit.
The Mengzhou can carry three astronauts between Earth and lunar orbit, with two of them riding the Lanyue lunar lander between lunar orbit and the lunar surface.
China’s Moon landing initiative will carry out, as planned, the Long March-10 carrier rocket technology verification flight, the first flights of the Mengzhou spaceship and the Lanyue lunar lander, and important missions such as the robotic Chang’e-7 lunar lander.
“When planning, we follow two principles,” Wang told CCTV . “First, for any task to be performed in lunar orbit, we will utilize the space station to conduct validation in near-Earth orbit whenever possible; second, for any crewed mission, we will try to fly it in an unmanned state first.”
To be utilized is the near-Earth version of the Long March-10 rocket to launch the near-Earth version of the Mengzhou spacecraft to perform space station missions in near-Earth orbit, added Wang, to validate the rocket’s basic technologies and the critical re-entry and return phases of the spacecraft.
“Then, we will use the lunar version of the Long March-10 rocket to launch the lunar version of the Mengzhou spacecraft to execute the lunar landing mission. This is a validation process for the rocket: near-Earth first, then the Moon,” said Wang.
Lanyue lunar lander. Image credit: CCTV/Inside Outer Space screengrab
The uncrewed flight mission of the Lanyue lander will allow for on-site collection of critical environmental data, including first-hand measured information on lunar surface temperature, lunar dust conditions, and the in-orbit performance of the spacecraft.
Wang said that the uncrewed flight mission of the Lanyue lander is also soliciting secondary payloads nationwide.
For a single mission, the total mass of the carried payloads will not exceed 50 kilograms, and the total power consumption will not exceed 100 watts.
“Because it is an unmanned mission, we will have some surplus resources, and we must make full use of them. Through a selection process, we will choose scientific experiment projects that are meaningful and necessary to be conducted on the Moon,” said Wang. “It is like giving them a ‘free ride’ to the Moon to conduct corresponding scientific experiments or technical explorations, achieving the goal of benefiting multiple parties with a single flight,” said Wang.

articles.title_orig: I tested Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo. It's a fascinating experiment, but the price is hard to justify.
articles.title_zh: I tested Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo. It's a fascinating experiment, but the price is hard to justify.
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
The iPhone Duo is designed to be compact, but that hasn’t stopped some from wondering how its size compares with other iPhone models .
Fortunately, we have all the current iPhone devices on hand to show how the Duo, when folded shut, stacks up against the dimensions of everything from the iPhone Air to the iPhone 18 Pro Max . This should give you a better sense of how easily the Duo might fit into a pocket or bag.
The iPhone Duo is a $1,999 phone that, in case it wasn’t obvious from the price, isn’t for everyone . With a 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display, it serves as a phone-tablet hybrid that’s ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working on the go. The Duo isn’t especially light or thin, but it’s also not too bulky. It measures 5.2 millimeters when unfolded and 11.3mm when folded, and it weighs 254 grams.
As a first-generation device, it has its shortcomings. The Duo doesn’t support FaceID, opting for TouchID instead. Its multitasking capabilities are limited compared to other foldable phones , and the cameras are more scaled back than the iPhone 18 Pro’s. But other details make the Duo feel refined and intuitive, from the matte texture of the inner display that reduces glare to dynamic software integration across both screens. The Duo can be a tempting option for anyone looking for a phone that feels refreshingly different.
Here’s how the iPhone Duo’s size compares to all current iPhone models .
Starting with Apple’s biggest nonfolding phone, the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. It measures 8.75mm thick and weighs 249 grams, making it just slightly lighter than the iPhone Duo, though that difference is negligible. What you will notice is how much shorter the Duo is, making it easier to slip into a pocket — even smaller women’s pockets.

articles.title_orig: Cyberattacks hit supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe, Belgium launches investigation
articles.title_zh: Cyberattacks hit supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe, Belgium launches investigation
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of supermarkets in Europe have reported temperatures of their refrigerators and fridges rising overnight, now widely believed to be caused by cyber attacks similar to the one that affected France several weeks ago.
Supermarket chains in Belgium, Sweden, Estonia, Netherlands, Luxembourg and Ireland have been affected.
The story began with Belgian media reporting on Monday that fridges were turned up to 17 degrees Celsius, forcing many stores to throw away food.
Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity (CCB) told Belgian outlet Belga that it is aware of an incident targeting supermarket refrigeration systems.
CCB spokesperson Katrien Eggers told Euronews Next, "We are aware of an incident, but have no further information." There are no reports yet as to who was behind the attack... and it may never be possible to identify them."
Belgium's federal prosecutor's office have opened an investigation into the incident, according to a spokesperson.
Some 40 Delhaize Proxy supermarkets, 15 Carrefour Shop & Go stores, 15 Intermarché shops and five Spar Q8 service station locations have reportedly been impacted in Belgium, according to Belgian outlet Le Soir .
Butchery group De Laet en Van Haver also said that their fridges were affected. IKEA have also said their Bergen shop located at Mons was affected, bringing the total to 75 stores affected in Belgium.
"We have identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen stores. We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational," a spokesperson from Delhaize told Euronews Next.
Carrefour told Euronews Next this morning that "the impact at Carrefour is very limited: currently 15 of our 700 stores are affected, both in Flanders and Wallonia. Not a single hypermarket is among them."
"All stores remain open because it only concerns a few refrigeration units, mainly freezers. Quick action was taken so that all stores can stay open," they added.
Meanwhile later this morning Carrefour Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen said, "It's a cyberattack, there is no other reason," adding that the "impact is very limited".
It's believed the incident took place between Sunday night and Monday morning, skyrocketing refrigerator temperatures.
Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration installer Sabcobel, which manages Delhaize's fridges and freeze systems, told the Belga news outlet that the Belgian attack involves exactly the same mechanism as the previous French cyberattack.
"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," Moelans said.
He said the incident happened when the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
The refrigeration executive said a software update alone is not enough to address the vulnerability, with physical modifications required instead.
"That requires investment. The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France."
Sabcobel know of around twenty affected units, out of the hundreds it manages across Belgium.
Danfoss, the company that supplied the software for the refrigeration systems affected in both the latest incident and the one in France in October, said customers who had not updated their software were affected.
A spokesperson told VTM NIEUWS that "the company says that the vulnerability lies primarily in outdated software and that they had already urged customers to start using their new software".
Problems reportedly also occurred at a number of stores of the Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop last night, with refrigerators and freezers turned up to 50 degrees Celsius.
A similar incident occurred in Estonian at one location of supermarket chain Selver, according to media reports.
13 SuperValu stores in Ireland were affected by a suspected cyber incident, according to a statement by owner Musgrave made to the Irish Times.
In the Netherlands, the freezing and cooling systems of at least seventeen companies were attacked last night, according to a spokesperson for supplier Danfoss. The identities of the companies were not disclosed.
Delhaize also suspended its ordering systems in Luxembourg as a precaution to prevent a similar incident.
Finnish media report that several K Group supermarkets have been affected. K Group is one of Finland's largest retail chains.
These reported incidents follow a similar attack in France just weeks ago, on 12 October, when hundreds of French supermarkets belonging to the Intermarché and Coopérative U chains fell victim to a cyberattack targeting their refrigeration systems.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.
The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.
The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title_orig: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
articles.title_zh: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
articles.content_orig:
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Seek Shot to Be Israel’s Premier
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Seek Shot to Be Israel’s Premier
articles.content_orig:
President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with representatives of the parties elected to the 26th Knesset on Wednesday, starting with the smallest factions in an unusual departure from previous rounds of coalition negotiations, the President's Office announced on Monday.
Rather than beginning with the largest parties, Herzog will invite faction representatives in ascending order of Knesset seats, beginning with Religious Zionism-Zehut and concluding with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud on Thursday evening.
According to the President's Office, the decision is intended to "encourage thinking outside the box," allowing Herzog to consider a wider range of potential coalition arrangements before consulting with the larger factions.
The consultations come as Israel's political parties face the challenge of forming a governing coalition following the October 27 election, with neither of the two largest parties, Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, enjoying a straightforward path to a 61-seat majority.
Herzog has emphasized the importance of exploring potential compromises to prevent another election, with the unusual consultation order potentially allowing smaller factions to present alternative coalition arrangements before the president meets with Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
In his statement, Herzog said he would hear the positions of all factions, seeking to "exhaust every possibility, broaden the dialogue, and explore any avenue that could advance the process."
The president also left open the possibility of holding a second round of consultations if necessary.
The consultations will begin Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Religious Zionism-Zehut, followed by Shas at 6:15 p.m. and Yisrael Beytenu at 7:30 p.m.
Meetings will resume Thursday morning, beginning with United Torah Judaism at 8:30 a.m., followed by Otzma Yehudit at 9:45 a.m., the Democrats at 11 a.m., and Ra'am at 12:15 p.m.
Following an afternoon break, Herzog will meet with the Joint List at 4:45 p.m., B'Yachad at 6 p.m., Yashar at 7:15 p.m., and finally Likud at 8:30 p.m.
During the consultations, each faction will be given an opportunity to recommend a Knesset member to receive the mandate to form the next government.
While the number of recommendations each candidate receives matters, the president is not legally required to select the candidate with the most recommendations. Instead, Herzog must determine which Knesset member has the best chance of successfully forming a government.
Under Basic Law: The Government, the Knesset member entrusted with forming a government has 28 days to assemble a coalition. The president may grant an extension of up to 14 additional days if necessary.
Should the designated candidate fail to form a government, the law provides for further procedures that could see another Knesset member given the opportunity to assemble a coalition.
The consultations will be broadcast live on the president's official social media accounts, allowing the public to follow the parties' recommendations and the opening stages of the coalition-building process.

articles.title_orig: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.title_zh: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.content_orig:
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.
Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."
Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from it's local councils".
In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.
Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided . Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.
Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.
Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.
Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.
Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.
It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise , arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".
The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.
Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.
In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".
One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.
Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".
Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.
In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.
"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.
"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".
Green Party co-leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."
She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."
In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."
It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".
"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.content_orig:
In "MALE ANT PULLS OFF OWN WING TO MATE WITH QUEEN," three minutes of raw carnality from the BBC Earth's YouTube channel, a fat, ponderous male driver ant unsheathes spikes in his abdomen to lop off his right wing, and then lets dozens of much smaller female ants squeeze him into the queen's muddy bedchamber. It's possible that some of San Francisco's famously overworked and undersexed AI researchers have studied this footage for tutelage. That is where comparisons between ants and artificial intelligence would seem to begin and end. But then there is Anthropic.
Last week, the company submitted a financial prospectus for what may be the largest initial public offering ever , and announced it would list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Anthropic employees also call each other Ants — "a nickname that captures the collaborative, ego-light culture of the team," it notes in its government filing .
ANT is marching onto a busy little hill of creepy-crawly capitalism. It's at least the sixth insect-themed ticker in stock market history, joining a squishy cohort that includes FLY, BEE, BUG, HIVE, and GRUB — each of which have fared far better in the wild than on Wall Street. In 2014, The Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba launched The Ant Group, a giant fin-tech player. "Small is beautiful, small is powerful," Ant Group founder Jack Ma said of the name.
Are there risks in associating a company built on code with a bug? We've heard from the economists. What about the entomologists?
"It's not very affirming," says Deborah Gordon, an ecologist in Stanford's biology department who has studied ant behavior for more than 40 years. Her book "Ants at Work" begins, "The basic mystery about ant colonies is that there is no management." Calling employees Ants "is not only saying there's no central control, but also that they don't even know what they're doing," she said on a video call, while a large printed photo of a carpenter ant lurked in her background. She also noted that all worker ants are female. "That's probably not true of the engineers at Anthropic ."
Andrew Suarez, an ant ecologist at the University of Illinois, was relieved that the ant story of the week wasn't "How do I kill them in my house?" and had some advice for the new breed of Ants. In ant societies, cheating "is a very good strategy when it's rare," and a terrible one once everybody does it, which is worth knowing for anyone deploying fleets of AI agents , he told me over video, while a mammoth trap-jaw ant from a poster for the sci-fi horror movie "Empire of the Ants" glowered behind him. Suarez added that some colonies settle border disputes without bloodshed: Workers size each other up and "stand on their little toes like stilts," and the side that looks outmatched withdraws. Perhaps debates among AI safety researchers could be settled on stilettos.
Rob Dunn, a professor of applied ecology at North Carolina State University, observed that a leafcutter colony can hold a million workers in underground chambers that "might read as small office cubicles," he said. "No worker would have a perspective on what's happening in a different cubicle. They just do their part." The queen serves namely to make eggs. "I don't know what the Anthropic analogy is," he added. "Maybe that's tokens ."
Some entomologists worry about how Ants may threaten ants. What will data centers' thirst for water mean for the red harvester ants in drought-stricken Arizona that Gordon has spent dozens of summers studying? What will their constant hum mean for insects that communicate through vibration? Others are seeking guidance from ants, rather than their bosses, on how to better use AI. Next week, Dunn is convening a meeting of entomologists to discuss what lessons scout bees and ants "might offer for thinking about AI models and AI agents."
Dunn began his career in the Amazon rainforest; now, he notes, if you search for "Amazon" you get page after page of results for the company. "Every biologist will have a sad day when they go looking for an actual ant and instead find an Anthropic employee ," he says. Paul Rudd (Ant-Man), Woody Allen (the lead in 1998's "Antz"), NBA star Anthony "Ant" Edwards, and the nu-metal band Alien Ant Farm may also be sad. "The deeper sadness is how few people are paying attention to the world outside the digital world."
In the insectarium at the American Museum of Natural History one late afternoon last week, thousands of leafcutter ants were doing thousands of things: slinking, circling, bonking into one another, falling upside down, drowning, crawling, pausing, tickling, sawing, huddling. Nearby, a mother sang "The Ants Go Marching" to her toddler. "Holy shit," said a young man watching an ant carry a leaf chunk 10 times the size of its body over its head while scaling a pole. Dunn had told me what to look for: individuals "doing absolutely the wrong thing," and scurrying yonder. That wiggle is how a colony finds a new leaf, a new path, a new tree, he said. "That little wiggle is really important."
Anthropic burst into public consciousness with an extraordinarily rapid gestation more common in the natural world than in capitalism. Founded just five years ago, it now stands on the brink of becoming one of the most valuable companies in the world. Many people who had never heard of it until recently now debate whether it will be responsible for the destruction of the planet.
Yet the real ants have achieved a scale that any tech company would envy. There are some 20 quadrillion ants in the world. If Anthropic had a dollar for every ant, the Ants would have to expand its expected $2 trillion IPO by 10,000. Ants have existed for 150 million years. "They will be around long after we're all gone," said Dunn.
Most ants have never been studied, Dunn said. A graduate student of his, who had gone out looking for ants after a breakup, photographed a vampire ant near Raleigh that had been seen only once before. It hasn't been seen since. "Even as we feel so fancy," Dunn said, the world is "fundamentally undiscovered." Also, he added as we were hanging up, ants are delicious.

articles.title_orig: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.title_zh: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
Chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg say fridge temperatures rose overnight, similar to hack of French stores
Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg.
A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”
French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.
Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.
Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.
Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.
after newsletter promotion
They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.
ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

articles.title_orig: America’s Gulf Allies Prepare for New Round of Strikes on Iran—and the Blowback
articles.title_zh: America’s Gulf Allies Prepare for New Round of Strikes on Iran—and the Blowback
articles.content_orig:
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title_orig: Englishman Karl Bushby returns home after 28 years walking 30,000 miles around the world
articles.title_zh: Englishman Karl Bushby returns home after 28 years walking 30,000 miles around the world
articles.content_orig:
Hull, England - For 28 years and one day, Karl Bushby took the long way home on an epic odyssey of human endurance back to northern England.
His adventure was made even more difficult - physically and mentally - with his two self-imposed guiding rules: he could not advance his journey with the help of any machine and he could not return home during the entire time, even if family or friends died.
It was also hardly a direct route. His journey was delayed at various times for months, if not years, by illness, visa restrictions in Russia, Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and having to swim massive bodies of water. His life was also threatened by armed gangs in the lawless Darien Gap in Central America, jail in Panama and a polar bear in Siberia.
Starting out at 29, he sported golden locks in his earliest pictures. Now 57, his beard is salt-and-pepper, and the elements and time weather his face.
On Monday, he took his final steps of an estimated 75 million to a hometown hero's welcome of claps and cheers as he walked into Hull, a gritty and proud working-class port city.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth. That's what it took to get me back," said Bushby to the assembled well-wishers in Hull, a working-class port city about 150 miles north of London.
"You wouldn't believe just how many people have been involved in this, to get us around the kinds of obstacles that we faced. We faced down governments. We faced down some of the hardest challenges. We've had to create two world records just to get back here. And I couldn't have done it on my own. So it was a world, global effort."
Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998. He made his way north through Central America, the United States and Canada, then crossed the Bering Sea to Russia in the world's first recorded attempt. He then carried on through Central Asia and swam for 31 days across the Caspian Sea in another reported first, in order to circumvent the war in Ukraine.
Over the past few years, he crossed Europe, and just last month, he swam from France across the English Channel, setting foot on the country of his birth where British immigration officers had set up to check his passport.
"It's almost like arriving in a foreign country," Bushby told CBS News over the weekend as he neared home. "I've worked with dollars for 28 years. I don't know the brands in the stores. So I'm going around wondering what I'm going to be buying. A couple of times I got caught out crossing the road because I'm looking in the other direction because these people drive on the wrong side of the road."
His home stretch Monday, quite literally, was a roughly 3-mile brisk walk from near Hull's town center to a quiet, sprawling neighborhood to the north of two-story, red-brick terrace homes.
Children lined the turn to his mother's home and cheered while an honor guard led the way.
Bushby pushed the cart that had been with him for about 25 years the last few steps.
He then embraced his waiting mother on the street outside her home. The cheers quieted, and the two shared a moment in this homecoming.
Bushby said he feels like a man wondering what home truly means after spending a generation around the world.
"I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long. And it's an odd feeling. And I almost feel guilt," he said. "Like there are other parts of the world now that feel more like home to me. And now I'm going to be faced with this weird static thing."
Now, after more than 10,000 days away, Bushby faces a different task: processing it all.
Confronted with the question of whether the world had gotten better or worse, he acknowledged the troubles but did not give up on his optimism.
"The world's in a little bit messier time; there are more wars, you know," he told CBS News. "But it's all good. At the end of the day, we've been through worse. So we all need to breathe a little bit, get through the tough times; we're going to be just fine. My bet is on us, no matter what. My bet is on humanity."
His final advice for anyone wondering if they could also accomplish something extraordinary: dream bigger.
"Yeah, you can, because I'm nothing special. Maybe we need the art of dreaming big again. People seem to dream outside of a very confined space mentally at the world that they live in," he said.
"You've got to have that little confidence. You got to realize that you're more capable than you think you are. People constantly underestimate themselves. So that's the first step, I think. Dream big. Realize you're probably capable more than you'd think. If you take nothing else from this … take that!"

Tech stocks aren't getting shredded for any old reason. It's actually very fundamental: Free cash flow is drying up for Big Tech leaders, and capex is rising dramatically.
Investors are questioning whether this ratio is totally out of whack, given more realistic growth projections for AI.
The combined capex of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft rose by $36.9 billion in the third quarter to $201.9 billion, the team at The Kobeissi Letter calculated (chart below). This figure has more than doubled over the past 12 months, and is up a staggering 356% since the first quarter of 2024.

At the same time, the combined free cash flow of these companies fell $33.1 billion last quarter to a negative $26.4 billion, its lowest on record. Free cash flow among these tech beasts has fallen by $88.2 billion over the last year. Only Microsoft reported positive free cash flow in the third quarter. Looking ahead, the strategists estimate these four companies plan to spend another $232 billion on capex in the fourth quarter.
The AI trade saw a serious slamming on Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about the weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech.
"The AI narrative is cracking as profitability concerns intensify," warned Miller Tabak chief markets strategist Matt Maley.

articles.title_orig: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.title_zh: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.
"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."
Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy said.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.
In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.
"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.

Iran's 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, resume nuclear talks
Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.
More than 300,000 Yemenis have fled fighting, UN says
The U.N. migration agency said the people are struggling to find shelter and life essentials, as aid groups face limited access to those in need.
They have fled as renewed fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces broke a four-year truce, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in one of the Middle East's poorest countries.
Taiz province, in southwestern Yemen, continues to take in displaced families, but many are fleeing south to Aden, which has now received more than 56,000 people, according to the latest figures by the International Organization for Migration.
“After years of conflict, families in Yemen are being forced to flee yet again, often with little more than the clothes on their backs,” Abdusattor Esoev, head of the IOM's mission in Yemen, said Sunday.
“They urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care. Without more funding, thousands of families could be left without the help they urgently need,” he added.
China to send special envoy to Iran and the Gulf
China said Monday it plans to send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters the envoy would focus on easing tensions and promoting regional stability.
The Gulf region “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict,” Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said on Monday, according to a readout of their meeting.
The move comes as China seeks to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region, which it depends on for a large share of its oil.
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two men in southern Gaza early Monday, according to Nasser Hospital, where their bodies were taken. One strike killed a man in his home; the other killed a man in a tent.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Major fighting between Israel and Hamas largely halted under the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes on Gaza that it says target militants, though the strikes regularly kill or injure women and children. Israel says Hamas uses civilians as human shields.
About 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, bringing the overall death toll to more than 74,500, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants.
